correctness.rationale: For every k, the multinomial distribution of a prime exponent across k ordered factors gives d_k(n)=product binom(e+k-1,k-1). Taking valuations at 2,3,5,7,11,13 in d2 and d3 produces the displayed exact 12x12 integer matrix A. Fraction-free integer elimination on the actual matrix gives det(A)=+1, so the exponent multiplicity vector is uniquely recovered for any number of prime factors provided each exponent is <=12. The profiles {2,2,13} and {1,6,8} give exactly (126,3780), proving failure at 13. The supplied standard-library certificate rebuilds the matrix, independently computes the determinant, and checks the collision and 399 direct ordered-factorization sanity cases. No finite experiment replaces the universal invertibility argument.

value.rationale: The question asks how much of an integer's entire prime-power exponent profile can be retained by only two low-order factorization statistics, a natural quantitative compression of recently studied full factorization polynomials. A determinant-one theorem gives a uniform, no-prime-support-bound reconstruction result, and an explicit first failing exponent 13 proves the cutoff is optimal. This is more than a value lookup or routine case count: the theorem locates an exact sharp structural identifiability boundary.
